To talk about life with a baby.
20 January. Kenji, Haruka and Sakura have just landed in Bucharest. Mihai greets them at the door, with huge bags under his eyes.
Mihai! We’ve just got here from the airport. Where’s the princess?
Asleep. At last. She fell asleep ten minutes ago.
You look terrible, my friend. How long since you last slept?
For three nights I haven’t slept more than two hours in a row. Rosa Elena wakes up every hour and keeps crying until Ana feeds her.
Ha-ha. Welcome to the club. Sakura cried for six months. Haruka and I stopped sleeping altogether.
I didn’t cry that much! Can I see her? I promise not to make any noise.
(from the bedroom) Come in, Sakura, but quietly. She’s about to wake up again.
(very softly) She’s so tiny… Can I hold her?
Of course. Sit down and put your arm like this, under her head.
She’s opened her eyes! She’s looking at me!
(from the doorway) Sakura’s started crying. Look, Haruka, your daughter has burst into tears.
I’m not crying… It’s just that she’s so beautiful. Ana, when are you going back to work?
In September. Mihai has already gone back to work, but only in the mornings.
Right, while we’re here, you two have to stop worrying. I’m going to start cooking right now. Haruka changes nappies like nobody else.
Kenji… my mum has been cooking for a week. The fridge is full of sarmale.
Then I’ll carry on cooking too. There’ll be ramen and sarmale. International cuisine, like at your wedding.

A verbal phrase = a helper verb + infinitive / gerund, which changes the shade of the action (starting, continuing, ending, repeating). Spaniards use them A LOT. If you use them, you sound natural; if you don’t, you sound like a textbook.
You saw “llevar + gerund” at A2. It says HOW LONG you’ve been doing something. The negative form is “llevar SIN + infinitive”:
Mi madre lleva una semana cocinando.

English says “I haven’t slept for three nights” or “I’ve been living here for a year”. Spanish says “llevo tres noches sin dormir”, “llevo un año viviendo aquí”. It’s one of the most common expressions in spoken Spanish.
Don’t translate “for / since” word for word: “No duermo desde tres noches” is wrong. Correct: Llevo tres noches sin dormir / No duermo desde hace tres noches.
Mihai has gone back to work (he’s working again).
“Volver a + infinitive” is the most natural way to say “again”, more natural than “otra vez”. Volvió a llamar = He called again.

to get down to something, to start
“Echarse a” is only used with a few verbs: llorar, reír, correr, temblar. “Ponerse a” works with almost anything: ponerse a trabajar, a leer, a cantar, a llover.

Ana writes to Grandma Rosario about what an ordinary day looks like now.
Grandma: you ask me what an ordinary day is like. I’ll tell you, but don’t laugh.
At five, Rosa Elena wakes up and starts crying. I feed her. At half past five she falls asleep again. At six she wakes up again.
At seven, Mihai leaves for the hospital. He’s barely out of the door when the baby starts crying again. Every time. I think she does it on purpose.

Elena is still living with us. She says she’ll leave “when the baby sleeps through the night”. At this rate, she’ll stay until Rosa goes to university.

Tres cocinas y una sola nevera
During the week Kenji’s family stayed in Bucharest, the little kitchen of the house in the old neighbourhood became a battlefield. A very tasty battlefield.
Elena had been cooking for a week when the Japanese arrived. She had the fridge full of sarmale, the freezer full of ciorbă and the larder full of jars of zacuscă.
Kenji had barely put his suitcase down when he started cooking. He had brought two kilos of noodles, three bottles of soy sauce and a knife wrapped in a towel in his luggage.
And on the third day Carmen arrived from Madrid, with a whole leg of jamón under her arm and a box of turrón.
Three cooks. Three cuisines. One fridge.
At first, everything was very polite. Elena stopped cooking when Kenji came in. Kenji stopped when Carmen came in. Carmen started slicing jamón in a corner so as not to bother anyone.
But on the second day the problems began. Kenji opened the fridge to put away a broth he had been making for twelve hours and found no room. Everything was taken up by sarmale.

Very carefully, he took out a tray of sarmale and put it on the balcony, where it was cold. Elena saw him. She didn’t say anything. But an hour later, Kenji’s broth was on the balcony and the sarmale were back in the fridge.

This happened several times. The broth went out, the sarmale came in. The sarmale went out, the broth came back in. Mihai, who was watching it all from the sofa with the baby in his arms, told Ana it was like a very slow tennis match.
“We have to do something,” said Ana. “They haven’t spoken to each other for two days.”
“Well, they don’t speak the same language,” Mihai answered.
“Yes. But they don’t even look at each other.”

It was Sakura who found the solution. On the afternoon of the third day, when Carmen arrived with her jamón, the situation was about to explode. There was no room left in the fridge or on the balcony.
Sakura came into the kitchen with a sheet of paper and a pencil and announced, in her best Spanish, that she was going to organise a competition.
“Like at the club in Madrid,” she explained. “Everyone makes a dish. Tonight we all have dinner together. And the judge will be… Rosa Elena.”
The three cooks looked at her. Then they looked at each other. And, for the first time in two days, they all burst out laughing at the same time.

That evening, the living-room table was full. There were sarmale with sour cream, ramen with egg, jamón sliced so thin you could see through it, and a mysterious dish that Sakura had made all by herself.
It was an onigiri filled with zacuscă, wrapped in a slice of jamón. Sakura called it “the three grandmothers’ onigiri”.

Everyone tasted it nervously. And everyone fell silent for a few seconds. Then Elena said something in Romanian. Carmen said something in Spanish. Kenji said something in Japanese. Mihai, who understood all three languages, burst out laughing.
“The same thing. All three of them said: ‘It’s really good. Why didn’t I think of that?’”
It was time for the judge. Ana brought Rosa Elena, who had just woken up and was looking at everything with her serious dark eyes. Sakura held a little of each dish close to her nose, very carefully.

With the sarmale, the baby did nothing. With the ramen, nothing either. With the jamón, she wrinkled her nose. But when Sakura brought the three grandmothers’ onigiri close, Rosa Elena did something she had never done before.
It was probably a coincidence. One-week-old babies don’t really smile, Mihai explained later, in his doctor’s voice. It’s a reflex.

But nobody paid any attention to him. Sakura was jumping around the living room shouting that she had won. Elena burst into tears. Carmen took out her phone to take a photo, but it was already too late.
And Kenji, very seriously, took a sheet of paper and a pencil and began to write down the recipe for the three grandmothers’ onigiri. He said he would put it on the menu of his restaurant in Madrid.

From that evening on, the sarmale, the broth and the jamón shared the fridge without any problems. And when Kenji’s family went back to Madrid, Elena and Carmen carried on cooking together, side by side, understanding almost nothing of what they said to each other. There was no need.
On the last night, before Kenji’s family went back to Madrid, Sakura stayed up very late by the cradle. Ana found her there, sitting on the floor, looking at the sleeping baby.

“You know what, Ana?” Sakura whispered. “When I was little, my dad was always far away. But now, when I look at Rosa Elena, I think she has lots of families. And that I’m a little bit part of her family too.”
Ana sat down beside her and put an arm around her shoulders. “You’re her Japanese big sister,” she said. “And you’ll have to come and visit her lots of times.”

Sakura smiled and didn’t say anything. But the next morning, before leaving, she left a little drawing in the cradle: three grandmothers cooking together in a very small kitchen, with a fridge about to burst.
